records.our_prose: Persimmon fruits reliably in the Rio Grande Valley: Valley winters easily clear its modest roughly 100-hour chill need, and Texas A&M AgriLife Extension reports both American and Asian persimmon adapted to most of Texas, including the warm south. Anthracnose and trunk canker in wet weather and heavier soils are the real variables here, not chill; native rootstock helps on heavier ground. Exact Valley bloom and harvest months are not separately published by TAMU; this window is conservatively carried over from the comparable warm, humid Gulf coast pattern.

records.our_prose: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring before bud break, or set a grafted container tree in the cooler months. Persimmon resents root disturbance, so handle the taproot gently and plant promptly. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, set the tree at the depth it grew in the nursery with the graft union above the final soil line, backfill with native soil, water in well, and do not fertilize in the planting hole. On heavy soil, plant on a raised mound for drainage.

records.our_prose: Non-astringent types (Fuyu) are eaten firm and hold at room temperature for a week or more, softening slowly. Astringent types (Hachiya) must be held at room temperature until they ripen to a jelly-soft, fully translucent stage before eating; rushing them leaves an intensely puckery, tannic mouthfeel. Persimmons continue to ripen after picking, so counter-ripening astringent fruit is normal practice.
